Modern.tagline: The line you used to see.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Picked over Grade A Creamery and Jersey & Oat — the cream line is a visible, photographable quality signal that consumers can immediately understand on a bottle. Grade A is regulatory and undifferentiated (every fluid milk is Grade A). Jersey & Oat hedges the dairy positioning awkwardly. The cream line is the single best visual cue for non-homogenized milk and the brand name shows the product.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern non-homogenized milk is a small but growing category — consumers reading labels are skeptical of ultra-processed food and the cream line is the original quality tell. The opening is for a glass-bottle DTC dairy that puts the cream line front and center in product and identity.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Straus Family Creamery (strausfamilycreamery.com) holds the glass-bottle organic premium slot. Ronnybrook (ronnybrook.com) is the northeast peer. Maple Hill (maplehill.com) defined 100% grass-fed organic milk. We sit closest to Straus with a sharper visual identity built around the cream line itself.
Modern.positioningStatement: Non-homogenized milk that shows its quality at the top of the bottle.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Cooks at home most nights. Reads ingredient labels. Already buys organic dairy at the co-op. Will pay $9 for a half-gallon if they trust the source.
behaviors: Buys glass-bottle milk and returns the bottles
Reads the farm's website before subscribing

dos: Name the breed and the farm
Show the cream line in product photos
List the homogenization status on every label
donts: Photograph the bottle without the cream line

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Picked over Guernsey Gold and Brown Swiss. A flagged that 'Beurre d'Isigny' is a protected AOP — pivoted to 'Maison Isigny Creamery' as A recommended. Isigny-sur-Mer is one of the most storied butter regions on earth (iodine-rich pastures, AOP since 1986) and the Maison framing places it in the haute-laiterie tradition without claiming PDO protection. Guernsey Gold is good but commercially less defensible (Golden Guernsey is also a UK-regulated mark in some contexts).
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury cultured butter and crème fraîche have become a quiet trophy purchase for serious home cooks and restaurants. The customer wants 84% butterfat, lactic culture, hand-paddled. The opening is for a maison-framed butter brand with Norman techniques and a small SKU range.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Bordier (lebeurrebordier.com) is the global benchmark for hand-paddled cultured butter. Échiré (echire.com) holds the Charente-Poitou AOP slot. Vermont Creamery (vermontcreamery.com) is the American luxury peer. We sit closest to Bordier with an Isigny-rooted lineage and a tighter range.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Cultured Norman butter and crème fraîche, made in the Isigny tradition.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 65. Home cooks who own a Lacanche or a La Cornue. Reads Saveur. Subscribes to David Lebovitz. Pays for butter the way other people pay for olive oil.
behaviors: Pairs butter with bread by appellation

dos: Name the lactic culture and the butterfat percentage
Quote butter in grams and on the cool side
Treat the butter the way a vineyard treats a vintage

typography.rationale: A neoclassical roman for the maison voice, a composed grotesk for the technical specs. The serif carries 250 years of butter tradition; the sans keeps the shopping experience clean.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Picked over Holstein. and Whole Milk Co. Cream Line is two words but it names the product's defining visual — the visible quality cue at the top of the bottle. Holstein. is too breed-specific and reads slightly cold. Whole Milk Co. is descriptive but generic. Cream Line is the most ownable: a noun phrase that becomes the brand and the product description at once.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimalist dairy positioning has shifted from descriptive ('whole milk', 'organic milk') to attribute-led — the single trait the customer can verify. Cream Line names the trait and the product in one phrase.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Straus (strausfamilycreamery.com) holds the glass-bottle premium slot. Ronnybrook (ronnybrook.com) plays the regional non-homogenized peer. Snowville Creamery (snowvillecreamery.com) sits at the same minimal-label tier. We sit smaller, with a single-line identity.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Non-homogenized milk, named for the only thing you need to know.

Corporate.tagline: Member-owned since the heartland was the heartland.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Picked over Pasteur Standards and Continental Creamery Group. The Wisconsin Dairy Belt is the single most credible US dairy geography (Wisconsin produces ~14% of US milk and has the densest cooperative concentration in America). Pasteur Standards is a clever anchor but reads more processor than producer. Continental Creamery is an importer position and loses the made-in-America B2B credibility. The co-op model is the most defensible corporate structure in dairy and Wisconsin is the canonical location.
Corporate.industrySummary: B2B dairy in 2025+ is dominated by a handful of large cooperatives (DFA, Land O'Lakes, Foremost). The opening is for a regional cooperative that competes on member-ownership and Wisconsin-specific geography to serve mid-tier foodservice and private-label retail.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Land O'Lakes (landolakes.com) sets the cooperative benchmark. Dairy Farmers of America (dfamilk.com) is the largest. Organic Valley (organicvalley.coop) holds the organic co-op slot. We sit smaller, regional, and Wisconsin-rooted.
Corporate.positioningStatement: A Wisconsin producer cooperative supplying foodservice and private-label retail across the upper Midwest.

targetAudience.primary: Foodservice buyers and private-label retail procurement teams in the upper Midwest. Values cooperative pricing transparency, regional supply security, and AOP-equivalent regional provenance.
behaviors: Requires SQF and Grade A certification

dos: Cite member count and farm count
Lead with Wisconsin geography and co-op model
donts: Imply scale beyond actual member roster

Corporate.logoDirection: A serif wordmark with a four-quadrant seal: a wheat sheaf, a milk pail, a cheese wheel, and a Wisconsin outline. Used on tankers, invoices, and the annual member report. The wordmark alone runs on digital.

typography.rationale: A serif for the institutional weight of a 100-year cooperative model; a grotesk for the operational documents and digital portal.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Picked over Cowbell & Curd and Pail & Churn. The Milkmaid's Almanac fuses two strong cultural anchors (Vermeer's c. 1658 Milkmaid and the agricultural almanac) into a content-led brand structure — the almanac itself becomes the editorial and product calendar. Cowbell & Curd is charming but reads as a single shop. Pail & Churn is more product-narrow. The Almanac scales across seasonal raw-milk products, farmstead cheeses, and a publishing tradition.
Creative.industrySummary: Creative dairy brands have a real opening in the seasonal-storytelling space — the calf cycles, pasture rotations, and cheesemaking seasons are all native to the product but rarely surfaced. The customer is reading Substack and shopping at the farmers' market.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Jasper Hill Farm (jasperhillfarm.com) holds the seasonal farmstead cheese slot. Cellars at Jasper Hill (cellarsatjasperhill.com) does the affineur position. Cowgirl Creamery (cowgirlcreamery.com) is the California peer. We sit alongside Jasper Hill with a publishing and almanac-led identity.
Creative.positioningStatement: A seasonal raw-milk and farmstead-cheese brand structured around a monthly almanac.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Subscribes to Salt + Spine and Cheese Professor. Plans a kitchen calendar around what's in season. Buys cheese by the wedge and milk by the half-gallon.
behaviors: Plans dinners around the seasonal release

dos: Publish the almanac every month with the release
Name the pasture rotation and the cheesemaker
